mechanism_narrative: A sustained increase in the federal funds rate over three consecutive months signals a tightening monetary policy stance, raising discount rates and reducing present value of future corporate cash flows, thereby producing negative S&P 500 forward returns over the next 20 trading days.
candidate_trigger: FEDFUNDS rises for three consecutive months
failure_condition: S&P 500 20-day forward returns are not significantly negative (t-test p > 0.10) during periods when FEDFUNDS rises for three consecutive months.

mechanism_narrative: A year-over-year decline in real personal consumption expenditures (proxied by GDPC1) exceeding 2% indicates weakening aggregate demand, which reduces corporate earnings expectations and leads to negative S&P 500 forward returns over the next 60 trading days.
failure_condition: S&P 500 60-day forward returns are not significantly negative during periods when GDPC1 falls by more than 2% year-over-year.

mechanism_narrative: A sustained monthly increase in the unemployment rate above 0.3 percentage points for three consecutive months signals deteriorating labor market conditions, which depresses consumer spending and corporate margins, resulting in negative S&P 500 forward returns over the next 20 trading days.
candidate_trigger: UNRATE rises > 0.3pp for three consecutive months
failure_condition: S&P 500 20-day forward returns are not significantly negative during periods of sustained unemployment rate increases above 0.3pp.

mechanism_narrative: A persistent monthly decline in the industrial production index (INDPRO) of more than 0.5% for four consecutive months indicates contraction in manufacturing output, which reduces corporate revenue expectations and leads to negative S&P 500 returns over the next 60 trading days.
candidate_trigger: INDPRO falls > 0.5% for four consecutive months
failure_condition: S&P 500 60-day forward returns are not significantly negative during periods of sustained INDPRO declines above 0.5%.

mechanism_narrative: A simultaneous rise in the federal funds rate and a decline in the Consumer Price Index (CPIAUCSL) of more than 0.2% in the same month signals a restrictive monetary policy coinciding with weakening inflationary pressure, which increases risk aversion and reduces equity valuations, producing negative S&P 500 returns over the next 20 trading days.
candidate_trigger: FEDFUNDS rises AND CPIAUCSL falls > 0.2% in the same month
failure_condition: S&P 500 20-day forward returns are not significantly negative when FEDFUNDS rises and CPIAUCSL falls by more than 0.2% in the same month.

mechanism_narrative: A concurrent increase in real personal income (PAYEMS) and a rise in the housing starts index (HOUST) by more than 2% month-over-month jointly indicate strengthening household demand, which boosts corporate earnings and drives positive S&P 500 returns over the next 20 trading days.
candidate_trigger: PAYEMS and HOUST both rise > 2% month-over-month
failure_condition: S&P 500 20-day forward returns are not significantly positive when both PAYEMS and HOUST rise by more than 2% month-over-month.

mechanism_narrative: A persistent decline in the unemployment rate below 4% for four consecutive months signals an extremely tight labor market, which increases wage pressures and input costs, ultimately leading to negative S&P 500 returns over the next 60 trading days as profit margins compress.
failure_condition: S&P 500 60-day forward returns are not significantly negative during periods when the unemployment rate remains below 4% for four consecutive months.

mechanism_narrative: A persistent monthly decline in real retail sales (RSAFS) of more than 1% for six consecutive months indicates a broad-based weakening in consumer demand, which reduces corporate revenue and earnings, resulting in negative S&P 500 returns over the next 60 trading days.
candidate_trigger: RSAFS falls > 1% for six consecutive months
failure_condition: S&P 500 60-day forward returns are not significantly negative during periods of sustained RSAFS declines above 1% for six months.
